sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Talquetamab, a bispecific antibody targeting GPRC5D, is approved for triple-class exposed (TCE) relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma (RRMM) based on results from MonumenTAL-1. We report updated indirect comparisons of talquetamab vs. real-world physician’s choice of treatment (RWPC) in patients with TCE RRMM.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: External control arms were created for three MonumenTAL-1 cohorts, two without prior T cell redirection (TCR) therapies who received subcutaneously administered talquetamab 0.4 mg/kg weekly (QW; n = 143) or 0.8 mg/kg every other week (Q2W; n = 154) and one with prior B cell maturation antigen (BCMA) TCR (n = 75) who received either schedule (median follow-up [mFU] 38.2, 31.2, and 30.3 months, respectively), from two real-world studies, LocoMMotion (mFU 26.4 months) and MoMMent (mFU 27.1 months). Imbalances in baseline covariates were adjusted using inverse probability weighting and multivariable regression. The relative effectiveness of talquetamab vs. RWPC was estimated for overall response rate (ORR), ≥ very good partial response (VGPR) rate, and ≥ complete response (CR) rate; odds ratios and relative response ratios (RRs) were derived from weighted logistic regression. Hazard ratios (HRs) for duration of response (DOR), progression-free survival (PFS), time to next treatment (TTNT), and overall survival (OS) were estimated using a weighted Cox proportional-hazards model.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: In the TCR-naïve cohort, talquetamab Q2W had significantly improved outcomes vs. RWPC; RRs were ORR, 2.58; ≥ VGPR, 5.01; ≥ CR, 52.22 and HRs were DOR, 0.52 (p = 0.0011); PFS, 0.47; TTNT, 0.46; OS, 0.35 (all p < 0.0001). Results were similar in the QW cohort. The prior TCR cohort had favorable outcomes with talquetamab vs. RWPC; RRs were ORR, 3.03; ≥ VGPR, 4.88 and HRs were DOR, 0.09, (p = 0.0004); PFS, 0.30 (p < 0.0001); TTNT, 0.26 (p < 0.0001) and OS, 0.37 (p = 0.0020).

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: With longer follow-up, these comparative analyses further demonstrate the clinical benefit of talquetamab over RWPC in patients with TCE RRMM, irrespective of prior TCR therapy.

tr.td: Patients with triple-class exposed relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma (RRMM) have poor outcomes and lack a clear standard of care, which highlights the need for new therapies targeting novel antigens to further expand the MM treatment landscape, both before and after exposure to B cell maturation antigen (BCMA)-targeting therapies.

In the phase 1/2 MonumenTAL-1 (NCT03399799/NCT04636552) study, talquetamab, a GPRC5D-targeting bispecific antibody, demonstrated robust efficacy outcomes and a clinically manageable safety profile, which led to the approval for the treatment of triple-class-exposed RRMM.

The objective of this study was to compare efficacy outcomes in patients with triple-class-exposed RRMM who were naïve to or had exposure to BCMA T cell redirection therapies treated with talquetamab in MonumenTAL-1 vs. patients treated with real-world physician’s choice of treatment from the prospective, observational LocoMMotion and MoMMent studies, with extended follow-up in MonumenTAL-1 and MoMMent studies.

bold.italic: What was learned from the study?

tr.td: Patients treated with talquetamab were significantly more likely to achieve clinical responses, especially deep responses, and had significantly improved progression-free survival and overall survival vs. patients treated with real-world physician’s choice of treatment in LocoMMotion and MoMMent.

With longer follow-up, this adjusted comparison further confirms results from previous analyses that demonstrate the clinical benefit of talquetamab over real-world physician’s choice of treatment in patients with triple-class-exposed RRMM with and without prior BCMA T cell redirection therapy.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Immunomodulatory drugs (IMiDs), proteasome inhibitors (PIs), and anti-CD38 monoclonal antibodies have significantly improved survival outcomes in patients with multiple myeloma (MM) [1]. Despite these advancements in treatment, MM remains incurable; most patients relapse and require multiple rounds of treatment [2–7]. Remission duration typically shortens with each treatment line, making the disease increasingly resistant [7]. Patients who have received IMiDs, PIs, and anti-CD38 monoclonal antibodies (i.e., triple-class-exposed) have a particularly poor prognosis, with no well-established standard of care and limited treatment options [8, 9]. Novel therapies, including B cell maturation antigen (BCMA)-targeting chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)–T cell and bispecific antibodies, have further expanded the treatment landscape of MM but have created a need for therapies targeting novel antigens, both before and after exposure to BCMA-targeted therapies [1, 10–14].

Talquetamab is the first G protein-coupled receptor class C group 5 member D (GPRC5D)-targeting bispecific antibody approved for the treatment of patients with triple-class-exposed relapsed/refractory MM (RRMM) [15, 16]. Approval was based on results from the phase 1/2 MonumenTAL-1 study (NCT03399799/NCT04634552), which evaluated two recommended phase 2 doses of subcutaneously administered talquetamab (0.4 mg/kg weekly [QW] and 0.8 mg/kg every other week [Q2W]) in patients naïve to prior T cell redirection therapy (TCR) and a separate cohort of patients who received prior TCR, including CAR-T or bispecific antibody therapies, at either dosing schedule [17]. Based on an earlier interim analysis with a median follow-up of 25.6, 19.4, and 16.8 months in the QW, Q2W, and prior TCR cohorts, respectively, overall response rates (ORRs) were 74%, 69%, and 67%, respectively [18]. Median time to first response was approximately 1 month in all cohorts and median progression-free survival (PFS) was 7.5, 11.2, and 7.7 months across the three respective cohorts. A clinically manageable safety profile was observed, with adverse events leading to few treatment discontinuations across all cohorts [18].

In the absence of a control arm in MonumenTAL-1, indirect treatment comparisons (ITCs) can be performed to assess the benefits of a treatment relative to regimens used in clinical practice [19, 20]. LocoMMotion (NCT04035226) and MoMMent (NCT05160584) are prospective, non-interventional, observational studies of clinical outcomes characterizing real-world physician’s choice of treatment (RWPC) in patients with triple-class-exposed RRMM [9, 21], which allowed for creation of an external control arm for comparison in MonumenTAL-1. Previous adjusted comparisons showed superior efficacy of talquetamab vs. RWPC in patients with triple-class-exposed RRMM who were naïve to or had exposure to TCR therapies including BCMA CAR-T and bispecific antibody therapies [22, 23].

In this study, we report updated results for the adjusted comparison of talquetamab vs. RWPC in patients with triple-class-exposed RRMM with longer follow-up in the MonumenTAL-1 and MoMMent studies. A subgroup analysis was also performed in patients with ≥ 4 prior lines of therapy (LOTs) to align with the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved indication for talquetamab.

sec.title: Patient Populations
sec.p: Individual-level patient data (IPD) from the MonumenTAL‑1 (NCT03399799/NCT04634552), LocoMMotion (NCT04035226), and MoMMent (NCT05160584) studies were used to conduct adjusted comparisons between talquetamab and RWPC. IPD from MonumenTAL-1 included two separate cohorts of patients who received subcutaneously administered talquetamab 0.4 mg/kg QW (n = 143) or 0.8 mg/kg Q2W (n = 154) who were naïve to TCR therapy. A separate cohort included patients who received either dosing schedule and had prior exposure to BCMA-targeting TCR therapy including CAR-T and bispecific antibodies, distinguishing them from the patients who were TCR naïve (n = 75; 3 patients from the MonumenTAL-1 prior TCR cohort were excluded as their prior TCR therapy was not BCMA targeted). Key eligibility criteria of MonumenTAL-1 were applied to the RWPC cohort to create an external control arm using IPD from the LocoMMotion and MoMMent studies, which included 175 patients who were naïve to TCR therapy and 36 patients who had prior BCMA-targeted TCR therapy. A pooled analysis was also performed in patients from MonumenTAL-1 (QW, Q2W, and prior TCR) who were previously exposed to any BCMA-targeting therapy including TCR therapies (CAR-T or bispecific antibody) or the antibody–drug conjugate belantamab mafodotin (an additional covariate for this pooled analysis) (MonumenTAL-1 n = 114, RWPC n = 57). All patients included in the comparative effectiveness analyses were aligned with key inclusion and exclusion criteria from the MonumenTAL­1 phase 2 portion of the study, which included patients with measurable disease as defined by International Myeloma Working Group (IMWG) consensus criteria, had received ≥ 3 prior LOTs (including IMiDs, PIs, and anti-CD38 mAbs), had progressive disease for ≤ 12 months since last LOT, had an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status (ECOG PS) of 0–2, and had adequate bone marrow reserve (defined as hemoglobin ≥ 8 g/dL) and renal function (defined as creatinine clearance ≥ 40 mL/min/1.73 m2). The index date for all studies was the date of treatment initiation. Median follow-up was 38.2, 31.2, and 30.3 months in the QW, Q2W, and prior TCR cohorts from MonumenTAL-1, respectively (data cutoff of September 2024), 26.4 months in LocoMMotion (final data, data cutoff of October 2022), and 27.1 months in MoMMent (data cutoff of August 2024). Detailed descriptions regarding data sources are presented in Appendix S1 in the electronic supplementary material.

MonumenTAL-1 was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and International Conference on Harmonisation Guidelines for Good Clinical Practice. All patients provided written informed consent. An independent ethics committee or institutional review board at each study center approved the study protocol (Table S11). The LocoMMotion and MoMMent studies were conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. All patients provided written informed consent. An independent ethics committee/institutional review board at each center approved the study protocol (Tables S12, S13).

sec.title: Efficacy Endpoints
sec.p: ORR, very good partial response or better (≥ VGPR) rate, complete response or better (≥ CR) rate, and PFS were assessed on the basis of IMWG consensus criteria [24] by an independent review committee in MonumenTAL-1, and by a response review committee in LocoMMotion and MoMMent. Additional efficacy endpoints assessed were duration of response (DOR), time to next treatment (TTNT), and overall survival (OS). Endpoints were compared between all three cohorts (QW, Q2W, and prior TCR) of talquetamab and RWPC.

sec.title: Statistical Analyses
sec.p: For the comparative analyses in patients naïve to TCR therapy, the inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) method, using the average treatment effect in the treated (ATT) approach with the talquetamab cohorts as target populations [25], was implemented to balance the prognostic baseline characteristics available in the RWPC and talquetamab cohorts. The IPTW-ATT method involved two main steps. In the first step, propensity scores were estimated using a multivariable logistic regression model by regressing treatment (talquetamab vs. RWPC) on a set of baseline patient characteristics identified as prognostic factors. These propensity scores were then transformed into ATT weights assigned to the RWPC cohort to make them comparable with the talquetamab cohorts. The balance between cohorts was evaluated using standardized mean differences (SMDs), where values closer to 0 indicate better balance, and values > 0.25 indicate violation of the balance assumption. In the second step, weighted logistic regression was used to estimate odds ratios (ORs) and response ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for response outcomes. Weighted Cox proportional hazards regression was used to estimate hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% CIs for time-to-event endpoints. Kaplan–Meier median duration estimates and plots (both unweighted [observed] and ATT weighted) were also generated for the time-to-event endpoints. The prognostic baseline characteristics to be adjusted for in the base case analyses were based on consultations with clinical experts; the chosen characteristics were refractory status, International Staging System (ISS) stage, time to progression on previous LOT, extramedullary disease, number of previous LOTs, years since MM diagnosis, average duration of previous LOTs, age, hemoglobin levels, lactate dehydrogenase levels, creatinine clearance, ECOG PS sex, MM type, and prior autologous stem cell transplantation. The fully adjusted analysis included additional adjustments for cytogenetic risk and race. IPTW using average treatment effect (ATE), average treatment effect in the overlap (ATO), and average treatment effect in the control (ATC) weights, multivariable regressions, and propensity score matching were conducted as sensitivity analyses.

For the comparative analyses in patients with prior BCMA-targeted TCR therapy (“prior TCR” cohort), as a result of limitations in sample sizes, only multivariable regression was used to adjust for imbalances. The base case covariates adjusted for included refractory status, ISS stage, time to progression on prior LOT, number of prior LOTs, time since diagnosis, presence of extramedullary disease, ECOG PS, lactate dehydrogenase levels, hemoglobin levels, and creatinine clearance in the base case analysis as covariates. Three sensitivity analyses were performed: one that included additional adjustments for age, sex, MM type, average duration of prior LOTs, and prior autologous stem cell transplantation (fully adjusted analysis), and two others that included additional adjustments for the type of prior TCR therapy (CAR-T vs. bispecific antibody) and receipt of a TCR therapy in the last LOT.

The same analyses for both TCR-naïve and TCR-exposed patients were performed in the subgroup of patients with ≥ 4 prior LOTs who were included in the phase 2 portion of MonumenTAL-1. This US prescribing information (USPI)-aligned subgroup represents the population indicated for talquetamab use in clinical practice according to the FDA-approved label [15]. In MonumenTAL-1, median follow-up was 38.0 months in the QW cohort, 30.5 months in the Q2W cohort, and 27.8 months in the prior TCR cohort for these USPI-aligned populations.
Analyses were performed using SAS version 9.4 (SAS Institute, Cary, NC, USA) and R version 3.6.1 and 4.0.3 (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria).

sec.title: Patient Characteristics
sec.p:
In patients naïve to TCR therapy, substantial differences (SMDs > 0.25) were observed in many of the variables before reweighting: the talquetamab 0.4 mg/kg QW cohort had a higher proportion of patients with immunoglobulin G (IgG) subtype (53.1% vs. 37.1%), extramedullary plasmacytomas (23.1% vs. 9.7%), prior stem cell transplant (79.0% vs. 66.9%), age < 65 years (45.5% vs. 30.9%), penta-drug refractory (31.5% vs. 18.9%), > 4 prior LOTs (55.2% vs. 41.7%), and progression on their last regimen in < 3 months (30.8% vs. 16.6%) compared with the RWPC cohort (Table 1). The RWPC cohort had a greater proportion of patients who were triple-class refractory only (excluding patients who were quad- or penta-class refractory; 23.4% vs. 10.5%) compared with the talquetamab 0.4 mg/kg QW cohort. Before reweighting, the talquetamab 0.8 mg/kg Q2W cohort had a higher proportion of patients with IgG subtype (53.9% vs. 37.1%), extramedullary plasmacytomas (26.6% vs. 9.7%), prior stem cell transplant (78.6% vs. 66.9%), age < 65 years (42.9% vs. 30.9%), > 4 prior LOTs (50.0% vs. 41.7%), progression on their last regimen in < 3 months (29.9% vs. 16.6%), an average duration of prior LOTs of < 10 months (26.0% vs. 15.4%), and an ECOG PS of 0 (37.7% vs. 24.6%) compared with the RWPC cohort (Table 1). The RWPC cohort had a greater proportion of patients who were triple-class refractory (23.4% vs. 16.2%) and an average duration of prior LOTs of ≥ 15 months (59.4% vs. 50.6%) compared with the talquetamab 0.8 mg/kg Q2W cohort. After reweighting, baseline characteristics were well balanced between the RWPC cohort (n = 175) and the talquetamab 0.4 mg/kg QW (n = 143) and 0.8 mg/kg Q2W (n = 154) cohorts. In patients with prior TCR therapy, differences in baseline characteristics were also observed between the talquetamab and RWPC cohorts: the talquetamab cohort had a higher proportion of patients with extramedullary disease (33.3% vs. 11.1%), penta-refractory (42.7% vs. 30.6%), and a longer duration since last TCR therapy (9.9 vs. 4.0 months) compared with the RWPC cohort (Table S1). sec.title: Treatment Regimens in Real-World Clinical Practice
sec.p: In patients naïve to TCR therapy in the RWPC cohort, 74 treatment combinations were used including PIs, IMiDs, anti-CD38 monoclonal antibodies, alkylating agents, corticosteroids, and various combinations of these agents. The three most common regimens were cyclophosphamide plus pomalidomide plus dexamethasone (16.6%), pomalidomide plus dexamethasone (11.4%) and carfilzomib plus dexamethasone (9.7%) (Table S2).

In patients with prior TCR therapy in the RWPC cohort, 25 treatment combinations were used. The most common regimens were cyclophosphamide plus pomalidomide plus dexamethasone (13.9%) and teclistamab (13.9%) (Table S3).

In the USPI-aligned population in the RWPC cohort, 69 treatment combinations were used. The most common regimens were cyclophosphamide plus pomalidomide plus dexamethasone (16.9%) and pomalidomide plus dexamethasone (11.5%) (Table S4).

Similar results were observed in the USPI-aligned population (patients with ≥ 4 prior LOTs) (Table S7). ORR (71.4% vs. 20.6%; p = 0.0003) and ≥ VGPR (57.1% vs. 11.8%; p = 0.0011) were significantly higher with talquetamab compared with RWPC. Improved efficacy outcomes were observed for talquetamab vs. RWPC in patients with prior CAR-T therapy as well as in patients with prior bispecific antibody therapy. In patients with prior CAR-T therapy, ORR was 70.9% for talquetamab vs. 40.0% for RWPC, with deeper responses observed in those who received talquetamab (Fig. 4). Median PFS was 12.3 months (95% CI 4.17–21.42) with talquetamab vs. 2.1 months (95% CI 1.15–3.48) with RWPC (Fig. S5a). Median OS was 28.3 months (95% CI 20.24–not evaluable) with talquetamab vs. 10.4 months (95% CI 4.14–not evaluable) with RWPC (Fig. S5b). Similarly, in patients with prior bispecific antibodies, ORR was 56.0% for talquetamab vs. 12.5% for RWPC, with deeper responses in those who received talquetamab (Fig. 4). Median PFS was 4.1 months (95% CI 2.86–7.66) with talquetamab vs. 2.6 months (95% CI 1.51–3.75) with RWPC (Fig. S5a). Median OS was 14.4 months (95% CI 8.15–not evaluable) with talquetamab vs. 13.4 months (95% CI 5.42–14.49) with RWPC (Fig. S5b). Comparisons between efficacy outcomes in patients with prior CAR-T vs. bispecific antibody therapy showed no statistically significant differences, suggesting that the relative effect of talquetamab was comparable in patients with prior CAR-T and bispecific antibody therapy (Table S8).

sec.title: Comparative Analysis of Efficacy Outcomes in Patients with Prior BCMA-Targeted Therapy
sec.p: In an additional analysis that evaluated all patients previously exposed to any BCMA-targeted therapy (including CAR-T, bispecific antibodies, and the antibody–drug conjugate belantamab mafodotin) across cohorts from MonumenTAL-1 and LocoMMotion/MoMMent studies, results showed superior outcomes in patients who received talquetamab compared with RWPC (Table S9). Results were consistent in the USPI-aligned population (Table S10).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Patients with triple-class-exposed RRMM have a poor prognosis, with no well-established standard of care and limited treatment options available [8, 9]. Recent advancements with the introduction of BCMA therapies including CAR-T therapies, idecabtagene vicleucel and ciltacabtagene autoleucel, the antibody–drug conjugate belantamab mafodotin, and bispecific antibodies, teclistamab and elranatamab, have improved efficacy outcomes in this patient population, with response rates in approximately 60% of patients with belantamab mafodotin and bispecific antibodies and higher response rates with CAR-T therapies (73% in idecabtagene vicleucel and 85% in ciltacabtagene autoleucel) [1, 10–14, 26]; however, the accessibility of CAR-T therapies in clinical practice remains limited because of increased logistic requirements. Talquetamab is a novel, off-the-shelf, readily manufactured, GPRC5D-targeting bispecific antibody approved for the treatment of triple-class-exposed RRMM [15, 16]. In MonumenTAL-1, high (ORR ≥ 69%), deep, and durable responses with a manageable safety profile were observed in patients who received talquetamab [18]. In the absence of a randomized controlled trial, ITCs using IPTW methods are an established approach to assess the benefit of a treatment relative to regimens used in clinical practice [19, 20]. A previous ITC was performed to estimate the comparative effectiveness of talquetamab in MonumenTAL-1 vs. RWPC, an external cohort created from the LocoMMotion and MoMMent studies, which showed superior efficacy outcomes of talquetamab over RWPC in patients with triple-class-exposed RRMM who were naïve to or had exposure to TCR therapies [22, 23].

We report an update of these adjusted comparative analyses with extended follow-up in MonumenTAL-1 and MoMMent studies for patients with triple-class-exposed RRMM. Results were based on additional follow-up in the MonumenTAL-1 study (approximately 20 months) and MoMMent study (18 months) for the RWPC cohort. During this time, the benefit of talquetamab over RWPC was maintained. In patients naïve to TCR therapy, the base case analysis showed a significantly higher ORR with talquetamab 0.4 mg/kg QW and 0.8 mg/kg Q2W vs. RWPC. In addition, risk for disease progression or death was reduced by 46% and 53% with talquetamab 0.4 mg/kg QW and 0.8 mg/kg Q2W, respectively, over RWPC. Talquetamab significantly reduced the risk of death compared with RWPC across both dosing schedules. TTNT was also longer with both dosing schedules. Similar results were observed in the fully adjusted and sensitivity analyses. These results are consistent with previous findings [22, 23] and further demonstrate the long-term benefits of talquetamab in patients with triple-class-exposed RRMM.

The subgroup analysis in the talquetamab USPI-aligned population (i.e., patients with ≥ 4 prior LOTs who participated in the phase 2 portion of MonumenTAL-1) showed consistent outcomes with the overall population. This subgroup represents the usage of talquetamab in clinical practice, as it aligns with the current FDA-approved label [15]. In both the base case and fully adjusted analyses, talquetamab showed improved outcomes across all efficacy endpoints assessed compared with RWPC. Notably, with 30 months and 38 months of follow-up in the QW and Q2W cohorts, respectively, median OS was not reached in the talquetamab cohorts, demonstrating the effectiveness of talquetamab in a heavily pre-treated patient population.

The introduction of BCMA-targeted TCR therapies including CAR-T and bispecific antibodies and the antibody–drug conjugate belantamab mafodotin has further expanded the treatment landscape of MM [1, 10–14, 26], creating a need for new therapies targeting novel antigens, both before and after exposure to these treatments. In this analysis, patients with prior TCR therapy showed significantly higher and deeper responses with talquetamab compared with RWPC. The risk for disease progression or death was reduced by 70% and risk for death by 63% with talquetamab over RWPC. With the addition of belantamab mafodotin to the analysis of prior BCMA-targeted TCR therapy, favorable efficacy outcomes were also observed in patients who received talquetamab vs. RWPC. In addition, efficacy outcomes were improved in patients who received talquetamab vs. RWPC following CAR-T or bispecific antibody therapy. In MonumenTAL-1, a higher response rate was observed in patients with prior CAR-T vs. bispecific antibody therapy (73% vs. 57%, respectively) [18]. Similarly, higher 12-month PFS and DOR rates were observed in patients with prior CAR-T therapy compared with bispecific antibodies (PFS, 50% vs. 30% and DOR, 55% vs. 43%, respectively) [18]. Although efficacy outcomes appear to be better with prior CAR-T therapy, the current analysis indicates the relative effect of talquetamab was comparable in patients with prior CAR-T and bispecific antibody therapy. Additionally, the sensitivity analysis showed a similar benefit of talquetamab regardless of timing of prior TCR therapy. The clinical benefit observed with talquetamab vs. RWPC in patients with prior BCMA TCR therapy supports talquetamab as a promising treatment option to fill the unmet need in this patient population.

Limitations of this ITC have been previously discussed [22]. One limitation we noted was the limited number of novel therapies included in the RWPC cohort due to their availability and approval timing with enrollment in the LocoMMotion and MoMMent studies. Although there was additional follow-up in these analyses, use of novel therapies was still limited and thus it remains a limitation to be further studied. Additionally, as a result of the small sample size in the prior TCR cohort, IPTW methods were not utilized as they have been considered unreliable in a limited sample size because of underestimated variance in effect estimates [27, 28]. However, alternative approaches such as multivariable regression, which was used in the prior TCR cohort, have been shown to be appropriate and are recommended for adjustment in this setting [27, 28]. This study did not evaluate the safety profile of talquetamab vs. RWPC as it was not within the scope of the study.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: In this study, efficacy outcomes in patients with triple-class-exposed RRMM who were treated with talquetamab (0.4 mg/kg QW or 0.8 mg/kg Q2W) in MonumenTAL-1 were compared with RWPC from the LocoMMotion and MoMMent studies, with extended follow-up in MonumenTAL-1 and MoMMent. Results from this adjusted treatment comparison confirmed previous results with improved outcomes for ORR, DOR, PFS, TTNT, and OS with talquetamab compared with RWPC. In the new analysis of patients with prior TCR therapy including CAR-T and bispecific antibodies, similar results were also observed with favorable outcomes of talquetamab compared with RWPC. The benefit of talquetamab over RWPC was maintained in the USPI-aligned patient population (i.e., patients with ≥ 4 prior LOTs who participated in the phase 2 portion of MonumenTAL-1) in both TCR-naïve and TCR-exposed patient populations. With longer follow-up, these adjusted comparisons further confirm results from previous analyses that demonstrate the clinical benefit of talquetamab over RWPC in patients with triple-class-exposed RRMM with and without prior TCR therapy.
